Perfect knowledge, or “wisdom” (Sophia), and philosophy as the pursuit of perfect knowledge
I. The ideal of “wisdom” as the ideal of conscious awareness

The way of directing human thought that we still like to call by the Greek name “philosophy” began, as everyone knows, in ancient Greece. The Greeks themselves believed that philosophy began with the thoughts of the seven semi-legendary sages, one of whom is credited with the famous saying: “Know yourself.” Socrates made this task—knowing oneself—his own. From him it passed through the writings of his great disciple Plato and became the central theme of humanity’s philosophical work, remaining so right up to the present day.
What, then, does the philosophical task “know yourself” actually mean?

At first sight, nothing especially complicated or difficult. It means not merely living and acting in the world around us, but also being able to answer every question that others can ask us, and that we can ask ourselves, about our life and our actions.
In other words, the philosopher does not merely want to live and “enjoy life,” as every living creature in some sense does. He wants to live consciously—in a way no plant or animal ever can.

The most obvious difference between the human and nonhuman worlds—although, as we will later see, it is only a secondary one—is that in the human world, and only there, we find what we call articulate and meaningful speech: conversation, or the exchange of questions and answers.
Animals and plants live just as human beings do. But only human beings also speak about their lives.

So the philosopher wants not merely to live, but to live consciously: to ask questions about life and, as far as possible, answer them. He is not satisfied with the life of a plant or an animal. He wants to live a human life.

In this very broad sense, philosophy is therefore as old as humanity itself. It began when the “first” human being asked the first question about his own life. And it will end only when living beings stop asking questions about their lives—or when the answer to every possible question of this kind has finally been found.

Experience shows, however, that not everyone is equally inclined to ask questions about life, and certainly not everyone is equally capable of answering them. These differences allow us to use the words “philo-sophy” and “philosopher” in their narrower and more familiar sense.

In this narrower sense, a philosopher is someone who, first, knows that questions can—and should—be asked about life and, second, makes the attempt to answer those questions an essential purpose of his conscious existence, rather than treating life itself as the only goal.

Naturally, the philosopher will ask more questions about life than the nonphilosopher. Indeed, the merit and “greatness” of a philosopher can be measured by the number and quality of the answers he gives to questions raised either by himself or by others.
The aim of philosophy, then, is nothing other than the experience of oneself: conscious life, the ability to ask as many questions about life as possible and to answer them as well as possible.

Put differently, the philosopher wants to live not only under the pressure of mute biological drives—his “instincts”—but also under the guidance of the rational principle of human life whose direct expression is articulate, meaningful speech, what the Greeks called logos: conversation, or the exchange of questions and answers.
Philosophy in the narrower, technical sense therefore means both the desire and the ability to ask questions and answer them, orally or in writing, through articulate and meaningful speech.
Its goal—its “ideal”—is the actual ability to answer every question that can possibly be asked about life.

The ancient Greeks called a person who could answer any question about his life and everyday actions a “sage” (sophos). They called the ability to give such complete and meaningful answers “wisdom” (sophia).

The Greek word “philo-sophy,” then, means nothing more than love of wisdom: striving for wisdom, desiring it, devoting one’s life to its pursuit, much as a lover wants to devote his life to the person he loves.

In one sense, we can say that if wisdom, or complete conscious awareness, consists in the ability to answer the questions raised by life, then philosophy, as the pursuit of wisdom or conscious awareness, consists in the ability to ask those questions.

Of course, the philosopher asks questions because he is also trying, as far as he can, to answer them. If he regards himself as a philosopher rather than a sage, it is above all because he knows that there is at least one question he can ask but cannot answer.
There is little disagreement among philosophers, and indeed there can hardly be any, that philosophy aims at self-experience, conscious awareness, or “wisdom.”

But once we ask a further question—can “wisdom” actually be attained by a human being who remains human, that is, by someone who continues to live in the real material world of nature, in space and time?—philosophers divide into two opposing camps. Some say yes. Others say no.
As we will now see, this difference is fundamental.
Before turning to it, however, we need to say something about another distinction that is just as important.

Philosophers have disagreed not only about whether their common ideal can be reached. They have disagreed even more sharply about the path that should be taken, the means or “method” by which the ideal can be reached—or, if it can never be reached, at least approached.
Here too we find two basic and opposing kinds of answer. The division is not identical with the one just mentioned, although it resembles it.

By defining philosophy as the ability to ask questions and the desire to answer them, we have silently assumed two things: first, that all these questions concern human life; and second, that human beings alone ask and answer them, without any help from something outside humanity.
In reality, some people whom we commonly—though, strictly speaking, wrongly—call philosophers see matters differently.
For them, the fundamental questions concern not the human being (anthropos) but what they call “god” (theos). And ultimately it is this “god,” not the human being, who supplies the answers.

What we are dealing with here is therefore an opposition between philosophy in the proper sense—discourse about the human being (anthropo-logy)—and the pseudo-philosophy more properly called discourse about god (theo-logy).
At the heart of this pseudo-philosophy, which is really a theological and religious outlook, lies the concept of revelation.

To define this concept philosophically, we can begin by saying that there are supposedly questions which do not arise out of human life and which an individual left entirely to himself would never ask.

We must then add that every chain of questions would ultimately end in silence, because the human being would eventually become unable to produce another answer. The missing answer would have to come to him from outside.

Finally, we would have to say that the rational and speaking being who is not human, yet who poses—or “reveals”—such questions to human beings and supplies—or “reveals”—their answers, is none other than god.
Wisdom, on this view, requires not only the philosopher’s own efforts but also divine revelation. Any complete answer concerning humanity must therefore also include an answer concerning god.
Theologians are divided in much the same way as philosophers in the proper sense.
Some believe that wisdom—which for them includes revelation and therefore questions about god—can be attained. Others deny that it can.

Those who deny it believe that there are questions which meaningful human speech can never answer. For them, god is ultimately unsayable (ineffabilis) and reveals himself only in wordless ecstasy. This is what is usually called mystical theology.

Others believe that, with the help of revelation, human beings can answer every possible question. Their god is as open to discourse as the human being is for genuine philosophers. We might, with some qualification, call them rational theologians.
But both groups have one thing in common: they assume that some form of revelation is necessary if wisdom is to be reached, or even approached.

That separates them from philosophers in the proper sense. Philosophers, without exception, believe that all questions that can be asked follow logically and necessarily from one another. It is enough to ask the first question suggested to a human being by his life, and from there either we can eventually reach the final question, as some philosophers believe, or we can go on progressing forever, as others maintain.
We must not imagine that this distinction between anthropological philosophy and theological pseudo-philosophy is the same as the distinction within philosophy between theism and atheism.
As we will now see, that second distinction comes down to whether one denies or accepts the possibility that a human being can attain wisdom.
It is true—and the word itself makes this obvious—that theological systems are usually also theistic. But this is not necessarily always the case, and there are exceptions.

If we call “god” whatever principle revelation supposedly comes from, then we can certainly say that every theological system contains some concept of god. But the word “god” then becomes unusually broad and vague.

It is difficult, for example, to say what exactly corresponds to “god” in early Buddhism, and it is far more natural to describe early Buddhism as atheistic. Yet it undeniably has a theological character in the sense just defined.

The same is true of “mystics,” ancient and modern, who work with ideas such as “inspiration,” “presence,” “intuition,” and so on. Strictly speaking, they cannot all be counted as theists, even though their openly declared theological orientation is beyond doubt.
In any case, the distinction that matters here concerns neither the object nor the goal of philosophy. It concerns its method.
Where “revelation” comes from—god or something else not ordinarily called god, such as the “subconscious”—is not the issue.
The issue is whether one recognizes revelation itself.

If someone believes that not all questions can be asked or all answers given without some kind of revelation, then that person belongs to the camp of theological pseudo-philosophy, opposed to philosophy in the proper sense.
We can therefore formulate the distinction as follows.

We can speak of “revelation” whenever certain questions or answers are not available to everyone, or whenever they require some special sui generis state unrelated to the normal development of discourse.

Alongside the familiar theology of theists, for whom revelation comes from god, we therefore find atheistic religions such as Buddhism, in which revelation comes from exceptional or specially gifted persons—“sages,” “saints,” and so on.
And we also find a nonreligious “mysticism” in which revelation is in principle available to everyone, but only under certain special and irrational conditions such as “ecstasy.”
On the other hand, philosophy in the proper sense is by no means always atheistic.

Theism is an error, as we will later try to show. But an error can still be philosophical, and experience shows that a thinker can arrive—mistakenly, but by an entirely philosophical method—at a concept of god indistinguishable from a similar theological or religious concept.

What matters is only that questions and answers concerning god should in principle be available to anyone capable of rational speech and in a normal, conscious state. Discourse about god must be logically connected with discourse about humanity and the world.
We must therefore distinguish atheistic or theistic philosophy from atheistic or theistic theology.
And the problem of these two kinds of philosophy brings us back to the question we raised earlier and postponed: can wisdom be attained?
What does it mean to say that human beings cannot attain wisdom?

Socrates already seems to have claimed that wisdom was inaccessible—or at least that is how his disciple Plato presents him. By examining Plato’s philosophy, we can see what this means and what follows from it.
